meta.title: Who really said "You yourself, as much as anybody in the entire universe, deserve your love and affection"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not the Buddha. It’s a modern paraphrase popularized by teacher Sharon Salzberg in her 1995 book Lovingkindness, loosely drawn from Udana 5.1.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You yourself, as much as anybody in the entire universe, deserve your love and affection'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the Buddha — a modern paraphrase popularized by Sharon Salzberg (1995), loosely derived from Udana 5.1, which actually says the opposite emphasis.

answer.label: Not the Buddha — a modern paraphrase by Sharon Salzberg
answer.authorDates: b. 1952 · American meditation teacher & co-founder, Insight Meditation Society
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording is not found anywhere in the Pali Canon. It was popularized by meditation teacher Sharon Salzberg, who presented it as a Buddha quote in her 1995 book “Lovingkindness” (an even earlier version appeared in “Woman of Power” magazine in 1989). It is a loose paraphrase of Udāna 5.1 — whose actual verse carries a different emphasis: because no one finds anyone dearer than themselves, one should not harm others.

source.heading: What the Buddha actually said (Udāna 5.1)

docMeta.dd: Lovingkindness: The Revolutionary Art of Happiness
Sharon Salzberg (1995); earlier in Woman of Power magazine, 1989

source.excerpt: Searching all directions with your awareness, you find no one dearer than yourself. In the same way, others are thickly dear to themselves. So you shouldn’t hurt others if you love yourself.
trail: Buddhist teacher and author Bodhipaksa traces the line to Sharon Salzberg’s 1995 Lovingkindness and an earlier 1989 appearance in Woman of Power, calling it a paraphrase rather than a genuine quote (Fake Buddha Quotes).
In Tricycle (Fall 2013) Bodhipaksa notes Salzberg likely adapted the wording from Mahasi Sayadaw’s 1983 booklet, which translated the Udāna using the word “deserves” (Tricycle).
The genuine source verse, Udāna 5.1, actually urges non-harming of others because each being holds itself dearest — a different emphasis from self-love (Access to Insight).
Quote aggregators such as Goodreads file the line under Sharon Salzberg, not the Buddha.
source.excerptNote: The canonical verse from Udāna 5.1 in Thanissaro Bhikkhu’s translation. Its point is the opposite emphasis of the popular quote: because each being holds itself dearest, one should extend care outward and not harm others — not that you should turn love toward yourself.

sourceLink.text: Read Udana 5.1 at Access to Insight

source.rightsNote: The popular English wording is a modern paraphrase first widely printed in Sharon Salzberg’s Lovingkindness (Shambhala, 1995), so it is in copyright. The ancient Udāna text is long in the public domain, but the specific modern translations shown (Thanissaro Bhikkhu; Mahasi Sayadaw) are themselves under copyright to their translators.

author.name: Sharon Salzberg
author.heading: Sharon Salzberg
author.bio: Sharon Salzberg is an American Buddhist teacher and a co-founder of the Insight Meditation Society in Barre, Massachusetts. She is best known for popularizing metta (lovingkindness) practice in the West, above all through her 1995 book Lovingkindness: The Revolutionary Art of Happiness, where this now-famous phrasing was presented as words of the Buddha. She studied under Burmese teachers including Mahasi Sayadaw, whose 1983 rendering of the Udāna using the word “deserves” appears to be the seed of the modern wording.

misattribution.heading: How a self-love slogan got pinned on the Buddha
misattribution.intro: The Buddha is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for uplifting quotes he never spoke. This one is a genuine modern insight dressed up as an ancient sutta.

items.why: Meditation teacher and scholar Bodhipaksa traces the phrasing to Salzberg’s 1995 book Lovingkindness, where it is offered as if it were a Buddha quote; a near-identical version appeared even earlier in Woman of Power magazine in 1989 (Fake Buddha Quotes).

Bodhipaksa suggests Salzberg drew on Burmese monk Mahasi Sayadaw’s 1983 booklet Brahmavihara Dhamma, which rendered the Udāna using “deserves” — a word absent from most other translations of the verse (Tricycle).

The real source verse, Udāna 5.1, uses the observation that everyone holds themselves dearest to argue for not harming others — not for turning affection inward. The popular quote inverts that emphasis (Access to Insight).

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: not a Buddha quote. It’s a modern paraphrase popularized by Sharon Salzberg (1995), loosely built from Udāna 5.1 — a verse whose point is compassion for others, not self-love (Fake Buddha Quotes).

context.heading: Why the mix-up is understandable
lead: The line is not a cynical fabrication — it grows out of a real Buddhist text. Udāna 5.1 recounts King Pasenadi and Queen Mallikā each admitting they hold no one dearer than themselves; the Buddha turns that honest observation outward: since everyone feels the same, no one should harm anyone else.

Sharon Salzberg, teaching metta in the West, distilled that idea into a warm, first-person affirmation about deserving one’s own love. The thought is defensible as a gloss on metta practice; the trouble is only that it circulates as a verbatim Buddha quote, which it is not.
context.pull: A real teaching, honestly reworded — then mis-stamped as scripture.
